title: Randomized medical-debt relief changes credit access without average health, care-use, or financial-wellness repair
source_unit: Participants in two randomized medical-debt relief experiments

denominator.unit: people receiving randomized-experiment debt relief; experiment populations differ by arm

observations.method: Two randomized experiments with RIP Medical Debt relieved downstream debt that had been or was about to be sent to collections; outcomes tracked through credit reports, collections accounts, and a multimodal survey.
observations.uncertainty: Selected collection portfolios and study arms; not all medical bills, care-forgoing respondents, or household debt are represented.
observations.subgroup: People receiving relief in the two randomized experiments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Treatment scale does not measure the share of all US medical debt or the amount reaching a typical household.

denominator.unit: randomized credit-reporting subexperiment; published average effects

observations.method: Randomized debt relief compared with control accounts under counterfactual credit reporting versus no reporting exposure.
observations.uncertainty: Credit access is not realized borrowing, housing, employment, insurance, or household recovery; effects are study-specific averages.
observations.counterinterpretation: Small credit changes may not be usable or sufficient to change downstream household security.

denominator.unit: randomized hospital-debt experiment; published treatment-control contrast

another_unpaid_bill_sent_to_collections.unit: percentage-point causal increase; 6.6% of 16.2% control mean

observations.method: Randomized relief at the point hospital debt would otherwise be sold to a collector; subsequent collections and care-use outcomes were tracked.
observations.uncertainty: The result does not identify intentional nonpayment, a general moral-hazard effect, or the original care-foregoing decision.
observations.counterinterpretation: Expectations of future relief, debt confusion, or targeting can affect repayment without changing care utilization.

denominator.unit: randomized hospital-debt experiment multimodal survey; published average effects

observations.method: Randomized debt relief with multimodal survey follow-up.
observations.uncertainty: Average nulls do not rule out heterogeneous effects; the design does not observe trust, political action, unpaid care, or food/housing trade-offs.
observations.counterinterpretation: Credit or payment effects can coexist with no average change in health or broad financial wellness.

boundary: This randomized remedy evidence begins with downstream medical debt and does not complete the chain from health need or care choice to household adaptation, trust, political action, or legitimacy.
